opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a fun question, because a quarter per query is actually a lot of budget compared to how we usually think about retrieval. Most of what we did with HippoRAG was designed around the constraint that retrieval should be cheap: you do the expensive LLM work once at indexing time, extracting triples and building the graph, and then at query time you run something like Personalized PageRank, which is fast and costs basically nothing.

If you relax that constraint, I think the first thing I'd do is let the model be much more involved in the traversal itself. Right now, PageRank spreads activation from the seed nodes in a fairly dumb way. It doesn't know what the question is really asking; it just follows the structure. With a long-context model and real budget, you could pull a large neighborhood of the graph around the query entities, say a few hops out, serialize it with the relevant passages, and let the model reason over that subgraph directly. It can decide which edges matter for this question, which ones are noise, and where it needs to expand further.

The second thing is iteration. A lot of multi-hop questions fail because the first retrieval step misses a bridge entity, and once you've missed it, you never recover. With a quarter you can afford several rounds: retrieve, have the model read and say "here's what I know, here's what I still need," then go back to the graph with refined seeds. That's closer to how a person actually researches something, and the graph makes each round much more targeted than plain vector search would be.

Third, I'd use some of the budget to fix the graph itself. Open information extraction is noisy: you get duplicate entities, missing relations, edges that are just wrong. At query time, when the model is looking at a local subgraph anyway, it can notice "these two nodes are clearly the same person" or "this relation doesn't make sense," and you could write those corrections back. So the graph improves the more it's used, which connects to the broader idea I care about: memory that keeps consolidating over time, rather than a static index.

The caveat I'd add is that long context isn't a free lunch. Models still get distracted when you stuff in a lot of loosely relevant material, and their performance on genuinely multi-hop reasoning across a big context degrades. So I wouldn't just dump the whole graph in. I'd still want the cheap structural signal, something like PageRank, to do the first pass and decide what's worth showing the model, and then spend the expensive compute where it actually adds reasoning. The graph tells you where to look; the model figures out what it means.

r001.rationale: The response proposes expanding neighborhoods around query entities and having the model assess edges, but does not propose selecting a graph entry point from thousands of candidate facts.

r002.rationale: It does not compare facts with entities as candidates for selecting an entry point or express a preference for facts.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about a relevant fact appearing among roughly 10,000 candidates in an internet-scale graph.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fun framing, because a quarter per query is actually a lot of budget. Right now with HippoRAG we're very conscious of cost, so retrieval over the graph is mostly done with cheap operations: embedding similarity to find seed nodes, then Personalized PageRank to spread activation across the graph. The LLM only touches things at indexing time, when it extracts the triples, and at the very end, when it reads the retrieved passages. The whole point is that the graph traversal itself costs nothing at query time.

If you gave me twenty-five cents per query, I'd move the language model much closer to the traversal. The first thing I'd do is use a long-context model as the thing that decides which parts of the graph are worth expanding. So instead of PageRank doing all the work, you'd pull out a neighborhood, maybe a few thousand nodes and edges with their source passages, dump that into context, and ask the model which of these are actually relevant to the question and where it should look next. That's basically letting the model do a kind of guided, iterative search, more like how a person actually browses a knowledge base. You take a step, you read, you reconsider, you take another step.

The second thing I'd do is spend money on reranking and verification. A lot of what goes wrong in multi-hop retrieval isn't that the right passage is missing, it's that it's buried among plausible-looking distractors. A long-context model can look at fifty or a hundred candidate passages at once and tell you which chain of facts actually connects the question to an answer. That's much better than reranking passages one at a time, because the model gets to see the relationships between them.

And the third thing, honestly, would be improving the graph itself at query time. Open information extraction is noisy. Entities get split into slightly different names, relations are phrased inconsistently. With extra budget you could ask the model to resolve those on the fly: "these three nodes are probably the same thing, merge them for this query." You'd be doing a little bit of schema cleanup every time someone asks a question.

The thing I'd be careful about is not just throwing the whole graph into a million-token context and hoping for the best. We've seen that long-context models still struggle when the relevant information is a small fraction of what's in the window, and the graph structure is genuinely useful for narrowing things down. So I'd keep the cheap structural retrieval as the first pass, and spend the quarter on making the model smarter about what to do with that structure rather than replacing it.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using a long-context model to choose relevant graph regions and where to search next, but does not say it selects an entry point from thousands of candidate facts.

r002.rationale: It does not express a preference for facts over entities as entry-point candidates.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about a relevant fact appearing among the top roughly 10,000 candidates in an internet-scale graph.

astra-6.text:
If I had a budget of twenty-five cents per query, I’d use the long context to give the model a much larger neighborhood of the graph to reason over. You’d still want an initial retrieval step to find the entities or passages that are relevant to the question. But instead of retrieving just a handful of facts, you could expand around those starting points and include the relationships and supporting text.

Then you can ask the model: Which of these connections actually help answer the question? What evidence is missing? And let it do another retrieval step if it needs to. So the graph gives you a way to organize and navigate the information, and the language model does the more nuanced reasoning about what matters.

I wouldn’t necessarily spend the entire budget on one huge context, though. I’d want to compare that against a couple of smaller, adaptive retrieval steps. Having room for more information is useful, but the important thing is whether you’re bringing in the evidence that connects the question to the answer.

r001.rationale: The response suggests an initial retrieval step to find relevant entities or passages, but does not describe having the long-context model select an entry point from thousands of candidate facts.

r002.rationale: It does not express a preference for facts over entities as entry-point candidates; it mentions both entities and passages.

r003.rationale: It gives no expectation about a relevant fact appearing within roughly the top 10,000 candidates or about internet-scale graphs.

sol-6.1.text:
I would use the long context to give the model a fairly large, relevant neighborhood of the graph. You still need a retrieval step to find some starting points—entities or passages related to the question—but then you can expand around those and let the model reason over the connections.

The interesting question is how to spend that context budget. Just adding more nodes isn’t necessarily helpful. You want to include the relationships and the underlying passages that explain why those relationships exist, so the model has evidence to work with.

With twenty-five cents per query, I’d also consider an iterative approach: retrieve an initial subgraph, ask the model what information is missing, and use that to guide another retrieval step. Then it can generate an answer grounded in the evidence it found. I’d want to compare that against simply retrieving more text, though, to see whether the graph is actually helping.

r001.rationale: It proposes retrieving starting points such as entities or passages, but does not say the long-context model selects an entry point from thousands of candidate facts.

r002.rationale: It does not favor facts over entities; it names entities and passages as possible starting points.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about a relevant fact appearing in the top roughly 10,000 candidates or about internet-scale graphs.
